title: A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation

concept.text: Proposed innovation: a neural interface that reads a person’s intended movements, uses those signals to control their body or an assistive device, and returns useful sensory information through a neural feedback channel. Its defining capability would be the sustained integration of movement control and sensation: the user could act and receive information about the action’s effects within a dependable feedback loop.

Conceptual scope: durability means preserving useful function during prolonged, repeated use, rather than demonstrating movement decoding or sensory stimulation in an isolated session. Recording, decoding, movement actuation, sensory encoding and stimulation would need to work together with acceptable safety and practical operating demands. The proposal does not require recording every neuron, restoring every natural sensation or repairing the underlying injury.

significance.text: Conditional significance: a dependable combination of intended movement and useful sensory feedback could give people with severe paralysis more natural control of their bodies or assistive devices. Feedback could help users judge the consequences of an action and make corrections, potentially reducing reliance on watching every movement. These are anticipated benefits of the proposed capability; their magnitude and clinical value would require direct demonstration.

The revolutionary advance would be a reliable, usable movement-and-sensation loop that supports everyday activity over time. If it improved independence, reduced assistance or made meaningful tasks easier, it could change the practical consequences of paralysis for some users. Broader deployment would also depend on surgical burden, maintenance, training, accessibility and the range of people who could benefit. A compelling laboratory demonstration alone would not establish those outcomes.

Limits on the analogy and downstream impact: an engineered feedback channel need not reproduce the richness of an intact nervous system to be useful, but distinguishable stimulation is not automatically natural or functionally helpful sensation. An interface may bridge disrupted pathways without biologically healing them. Memory restoration and broader human–AI integration would require separate advances; neither follows from successful movement control with sensory feedback.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed capability gap: the missing advance is sustained, integrated performance across neural recording, movement decoding, precise stimulation, useful sensory coding and practical operation. Success in any one component would not establish the complete interface. The engineering challenge is to preserve the usefulness of the whole loop as the user, recorded signals and implanted system change over time.

Engineering synthesis: concrete barriers include maintaining usable recordings, keeping stimulation sufficiently selective, translating device or body state into feedback the user can interpret, and managing interference between recording and stimulation. Long-term implantation must also be evaluated for tissue effects and device failure. Practical wireless operation introduces additional demands for power, communication reliability and manageable equipment. These are proposed engineering considerations, not requirements verified by the retained scientific source.

Scope clarification: recording millions of neurons with no foreign-body response is a speculative engineering specification, not an established prerequisite for this innovation. The necessary recording scale, acceptable tissue response and stimulation precision should be determined by functional benefit and safety evidence. The supplied materials do not establish a numerical channel requirement, a validated biological-response threshold or a particular architecture that would be sufficient.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes a 2023 result to Lorach and colleagues in “Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface.” It describes one person with chronic spinal cord injury whose decoded cortical activity controlled spinal stimulation for standing and walking. This remains a dated report attributed by the supplied research: the retained source material available to the review did not permit verification of the paper’s identity, participant count, injury history, control method or walking outcome.

The source-access limitation is material. According to the supplied review, the retained HTML contained only a cookie-access notice, with no inspectable abstract or article text. The earlier assertion that the result rested on an indexed abstract therefore cannot be sustained from these materials. Although the source index records a saved artifact, that does not establish that scientific content was successfully retained. This evidence gap does not show that the attributed result is false.

Conditional interpretation of the attributed result: if verified as described, a one-person brain–spine demonstration would support the feasibility of a neural bridge for movement. It would not, by itself, establish the proposed integrated sensory-feedback capability, generalization across causes of paralysis, broad independent use or deployment at scale. No inspectable scientific findings in the supplied record establish completion of the durable bidirectional interface.

Coverage limitation: the supplied review reports no bounded freshness-search record establishing developments through 2026-11-01. The materials therefore cannot support a comprehensive account of the field at that date or resolve whether subsequent work materially changed its position. Missing coverage does not contradict the attributed 2023 report.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration framework: multicenter studies should show sustained, independent use for varied everyday movement tasks with useful, distinguishable sensory feedback. Studies should include people with different causes of paralysis and report outcomes by participant and clinical context, so that success in a narrow group is not mistaken for broad applicability. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Multicenter sustained independent everyday movement with useful distinguishable sensory feedback

completion_criteria.text: Proposed tests of sensory contribution: controlled comparisons should assess movement performance with and without informative feedback under otherwise comparable conditions. Evaluation should distinguish the ability to detect or discriminate stimulation from the ability to use it to improve an action. Appropriate measures could include task success, errors, assistance required, correction of unexpected disturbances and user effort. The protocol should specify meaningful benefits in advance rather than treating any measurable difference as sufficient.
completion_criteria.label: Informative sensory feedback improves movement performance by prespecified meaningful criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and reproducibility tests: follow-up should establish how function and safety change over time, including interruptions, recalibration, training, maintenance and any repeat procedures. Reports should make clear which tasks users perform independently and what technical or caregiver support remains necessary. Replication across participants, centers and operators would provide stronger evidence than repeated success under one team’s supervision. Definitions of sustained use, useful feedback and acceptable risk should be set prospectively and justified for the intended application; the supplied materials establish no particular duration or numerical threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Longitudinal function, safety and support requirements are documented

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: a convincing demonstration should identify supported movements, sensory channels, environments and patient groups, together with failure conditions and operational burdens. Finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality across all movements, sensations or forms of paralysis. Completion would not imply biological repair, restoration of every natural sensation or suitability for every patient.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated operating boundaries, failure conditions and operational burdens are identified

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison with NRL-07, “A dependable neural communication channel for profound paralysis”: both concepts concern dependable access to neural signals for people with severe motor impairment. NRL-07’s stated goal is communication; NRL-17’s is movement control coupled to sensory feedback. They could share interface and reliability advances, but success in communication would not establish effective movement-and-sensation control, or vice versa. Only the neighboring concept’s title was supplied, so its detailed design and evidence cannot be compared.

Roster-based comparison with NRL-05, “Regenerate a severely injured spinal cord with functional reconnection”: both could address consequences of spinal cord injury, but their central mechanisms differ. NRL-05 proposes biological reconnection; NRL-17 proposes an engineered interface that could bridge disrupted function. Either could potentially complement the other, but neither capability follows automatically from the other. NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” likewise concerns biological replacement and preservation of function rather than the proposed interface loop.

Roster-based comparison with NRL-03, “Whole-brain, cellular-resolution recording during natural behavior,” and NRL-02, “A general predictive theory of neural circuit computation”: advances in recording or understanding neural computation could inform interface design. Their goals remain distinct. NRL-17 does not establish a need for whole-brain cellular recording or a general theory of neural computation; its proposed success is defined by useful, durable function within a specified application.

Roster-based comparison with NRL-08, “A visual-cortex prosthesis that restores useful, detailed sight”: both involve supplying useful information through neural stimulation, but NRL-08 targets visual perception, whereas NRL-17 couples feedback to movement control. NRL-16, “Biologically repair the injured visual pathway,” instead targets biological repair. Shared challenges in useful sensory coding do not make these interchangeable capabilities.

Roster-based comparison with NRL-04, “Read and selectively repair the physical traces of specific memories”: accessing movement-related signals and delivering sensory feedback would not establish access to specific memory traces or the ability to repair them. Memory restoration remains a separate capability. These comparisons preserve the roster entries as distinct proposals and do not infer their achievement or detailed requirements from their titles.

unresolved_issues: The retained artifact does not verify the cited paper’s identity or the attributed participant count, chronic injury history, stimulation-control method and standing or walking outcomes.
No inspectable scientific text in the supplied materials documents the underlying integrated-interface goal or establishes its detailed engineering requirements.
The supplied record does not establish developments through 2026-11-01 or whether later work changes the assessment.
Required recording scale, useful sensory information, acceptable tissue response and sufficient stimulation selectivity remain unspecified.
Appropriate durations, functional benefit thresholds, safety boundaries and acceptable maintenance burdens require prospective justification for the intended users and application.
Detailed evidence and designs for neighboring roster concepts were not supplied; comparisons are limited to their titles and the conceptual relationships described in the research and review.

brief.title: Lasting movement control with a sense of touch
possible: People with severe paralysis could control their own limbs or an assistive device through intended movement and receive useful sensations in return. A neural interface—a system that reads and stimulates the nervous system—would keep movement and sensation working together through repeated everyday use.
why: Sensory feedback could help users judge what a movement achieved and correct mistakes without watching every action. Dependable control could make daily tasks easier and reduce the help some people need.
The benefit depends on the whole system remaining useful over time, with manageable surgery, training and maintenance. It would bridge disrupted nerve pathways without necessarily healing the injury.

sources.showed: They reported that brain signals controlled electrical stimulation of the spinal cord, enabling standing and walking in one person with spinal cord injury.
sources.cited_for: The work supports the feasibility of linking movement intentions to spinal stimulation.
sources.not_established: Movement control alone does not establish useful sensory feedback or dependable everyday use.

sources.who: Santosh Chandrasekaran and colleagues at Northwell Health and collaborators
sources.showed: In one person with paralysis of all limbs, a system linked intended hand movements with stimulation and touch feedback. It enabled self-feeding, drinking and handling delicate objects.
sources.quote: this hybrid approach enabled recovery of functional abilities including self-feeding and manipulation of delicate objects
sources.cited_for: The work shows movement and sensation combined in the user's own hand, with benefits during practical tasks.
sources.not_established: A single participant does not establish dependable use across people, settings and causes of paralysis.

sources.who: Sharlene N. Flesher and colleagues at the University of Pittsburgh
sources.showed: A person with paralysis of all limbs controlled a robotic arm through brain signals. Adding touch sensations through brain stimulation halved task completion times.
sources.quote: Faster times were primarily due to less time spent attempting to grasp objects, revealing that mimicking known biological control principles results in task performance that is closer to healthy human abilities.
sources.cited_for: The work shows that artificial touch can improve movement performance beyond control using vision alone.
sources.not_established: The study does not establish sustained independent everyday use across users.

sources.who: Jeffrey Lim and colleagues at UCI, USC, Caltech and collaborators
sources.showed: One participant with epilepsy and no paralysis controlled a powered walking frame through brain signals while receiving artificial sensations from both legs.
sources.quote:
This study establishes the feasibility of an embedded system BDBCI for restoring both motor control 
and artificial sensation of walking.
sources.cited_for: The work shows that brain-controlled stepping and artificial leg sensations can operate together.
sources.not_established: It does not establish benefit for people with paralysis, improved walking from feedback or lasting everyday use.

shown: Northwell Health researchers and collaborators combined control of a participant's own hand with touch feedback, enabling practical tasks. Their movement-reading software maintained consistent performance over five months. That is progress toward durability, but it does not establish lasting reliability of the whole system.
missing: Studies across centers and causes of paralysis must show sustained, independent everyday movement with useful sensory feedback.
Controlled tests must show that feedback improves actions by a meaningful amount, beyond merely producing detectable sensations.
Long-term studies must establish safety, reliability, support needs and the conditions in which the complete system fails.

milestones.label: Independent everyday movement and useful sensation across centers
milestones.explanation: Studies across centers must show sustained independent everyday tasks with distinguishable, useful feedback in people with different causes of paralysis. This would establish benefit beyond a narrow group.

milestones.label: Sensory feedback meaningfully improves movement
milestones.explanation: Comparable tests with and without informative feedback must meet meaningful benefit criteria set in advance. This would show that sensation helps users act, rather than merely letting them detect stimulation.

milestones.label: Lasting function, safety and support needs are documented
milestones.explanation: Follow-up must track function, safety, interruptions and support needs, with replication across people, centers and operators. This would establish durability and show how much help independent use requires.

milestones.label: Operating limits, failures and practical burdens are established
milestones.explanation: Testing must identify supported movements, sensations, environments and patient groups, alongside failures and operating burdens. This would establish where the system is useful and where its demonstrated capability ends.

uncertain: How long must useful function last, and how much improvement would justify the risks and maintenance?
How many brain signals and how precise a stimulation pattern are needed for safe, useful control?
Which sensory information helps most, and how widely will benefits extend across causes of paralysis?
